old: in a 1-3-1 F1 pressures and three lock the neutral zone, which is a trap
new: in a neutral-zone 1-3-1 F1 pressures and three hold the middle third, which is a trap
note: Voiced alone in a dump-in retrieval list, 'a 1-3-1' here is the forecheck, and the line tells its three to sit in the neutral zone. The owner, forechecking_systems.md:421-447, says the 1-3-1 forecheck is pushed up into their end: its line of three is F2, F3 and one defenceman, shifting with the puck so the puck-side player is 'an immediate second attacker'. Glossary :264 agrees ('pressuring in the opponent's end'). 147->~150 of 200 chars. 'lock' also collides with the left-wing lock.

old: In a **1-3-1 forecheck** F1 pressures and three players lock the neutral zone, which is barely a forecheck at all — it is a trap.
new: In a **neutral-zone 1-3-1** F1 pressures and three players hold the middle third, which is barely a forecheck at all — it is a trap. Pushed up into their end, the 1-3-1 forecheck in [Forechecking Systems](forechecking_systems.md) attacks with the puck-side player of its three.
note: It names the 1-3-1 forecheck explicitly and calls it a trap, contradicting the owner's heading '1-3-1 — the modern trap-adjacent forecheck' (FS:421) and its pushed-up version (FS:447). The facts twin is :879.

old: two means space to attack, three means a 1-3-1, four in a line means a 1-4 or a full trap
new: two means a 1-2-2, so read F1 before you attack — its trap waits at the red line; three means a 1-3-1, four in a line a 1-4
note: Voiced alone, 'two means space to attack' sends a carrier into this page's own 1-2-2 trap. NZ:163/:170 and the caption nz-1-2-2-trap put exactly two, F2 and F3, across at the red line to kill the carrier who is 'allowed to skate'. 'A full trap' has four in a line, which no trap on this page does (the trap is 2+2). Also, three across can be the left-wing lock's back line (NZ:288, :292), which has no ice behind it, as well as a 1-3-1. ~126->~125 of 200.

old: Countered by: A 1-3-1, which exists to kill the stretch pass; a conservative 1-2-2
new: Countered by: A 1-3-1 if your stretch man is not already behind its line; a conservative 1-2-2
note: This contradicts the owner on the same shape in the same zone. NZ, which calls itself the authority on the neutral-zone 1-3-1 (FS:301, :447), says the stretch pass COUNTERS a 1-3-1: facts :653, body :660, ':764 Stretch a forward behind the wall — against a 1-3-1', and ':840 Against a 1-3-1 the stretch pass is live'. Breakouts says the 1-3-1 kills it. A defenceman reading one page or the other makes the opposite decision. The sketch is a reconciling guess; the owner must decide which reading stands. 157->~165 of 200.

old: Key: The 1-3-1 takes away every long pass — the stretch is dead
new: Key: The 1-3-1 takes away the long pass through it — a stretch only works to a forward already behind its line
note: The same contradiction as :459, in the 'Against a 1-3-1' block, voiced alone. NZ:840 says the opposite in its own reading list. 147 chars of 200, so check room.

old: Key: Umbrella — you are one of two defencemen high, so you have a point partner and can play give-and-go across the top
new: Key: Umbrella — in the classic version you are one of two defencemen on the flanks with a partner; in the modern one you are the lone defenceman at the apex
note: The owner, special_teams.md:147 and :156, has two umbrellas: classic, with a forward apex and both D on the flanks, and modern, with the lone D at the apex and two forwards at the tops of the circles. The pp-umbrella caption draws the MODERN one as the umbrella picture ('the lone defenceman takes the apex'). Four-forward first units are measured at about 56% of 5-on-4 ice time (ST:123), so a defenceman told he has a point partner may have none. 114->~155 of 200.

old: - **Umbrella:** you are one of two defencemen high, so you *do* have a point partner and can play give-and-go across the top.
new: - **Umbrella:** in the classic version you are one of two defencemen on the flanks, so you *do* have a point partner and can play give-and-go across the top; in the modern version you are the lone defenceman at the apex, with forwards on the flanks.
note: The body twin of :695. Section :702 frames the question as 'whether you have a partner up there', so the wrong answer is exactly the one this bullet gives.

old: - **Two** → there is space. Attack it.
new: - **Two** → a 1-2-2. There is space if F1 is closing; if they sit back at the red line it is the trap, so do not skate into them.
note: The body twin of :828. Read 1 (:839) mentions a trap, but this bullet stands alone in its own list. :845 'Four in a line → 1-4 or a full trap' also uses a 'full trap' the page never defines.

old: A 1-3-1 exists to kill it — three players stretched across the neutral zone erase the lane.
new: A 1-3-1 kills a stretch thrown into its line — though a forward already behind that line is what beats it ([Neutral Zone Systems](neutral_zone_systems.md)).
note: The body twin of :459. It contradicts NZ:764.

old: every long pass. The stretch is dead, the cross-ice over is dead
new: every long pass through it. A stretch into the line is dead unless your forward is already behind it; the cross-ice over is dead
note: The body twin of :745.

old: In an umbrella or an overload you are low or on the strong-side wall, so ask which your team runs.
new: In an umbrella or an overload you are usually low or on the strong-side wall — in a modern umbrella you may be a flank at the top of a circle — so ask which your team runs.
note: A Key Takeaway, voiced alone, that drops the body's 'usually' (:588, :600). In ST's modern umbrella (:147, :156, pp-umbrella caption) two forwards are the flanks at the tops of the circles. A centre there is neither low nor on the wall.

old: an aggressive 1-2-2 press wants you challenging the line, a 1-3-1 trap wants you holding
new: an aggressive neutral-zone press behind a 2-1-2 forecheck wants you challenging the line, a 1-3-1 or 1-2-2 trap wants you holding
note: The owner, NZ:128 and :152, calls the 1-2-2 'the classic containment structure… the safest to teach', and puts pressure behind a 2-1-2 forecheck (NZ:230-244). A defenceman whose team 'plays a 1-2-2', the rec default, hears that he should challenge at the line. Siblings center.md:265 and defender.md:412/:422 already use 'press… behind a 2-1-2'. NZ:838 does mention 'an aggressive 1-2-2', so this is a naming fix, not a factual one. 148->~170 of 300.

old: A team playing an aggressive 1-2-2 neutral-zone press wants you challenging at the line
new: A team playing an aggressive neutral-zone press behind a 2-1-2 forecheck wants you challenging at the line
note: The same as :789.

old: a team playing an aggressive 1-2-2 neutral-zone press wants you challenging at the line
new: a team playing an aggressive neutral-zone press behind a 2-1-2 forecheck wants you challenging at the line
note: The same as :789.

old: The pure 1-3-1 trap is far rarer now than its reputation suggests; most teams use trap *elements*, such as a 1-2-2 with a heavy middle.
new: The pure passive trap is far rarer now than its reputation suggests; most teams use trap *elements* instead.
note: This calls the 1-3-1 the rare 'pure trap'. The owner says the opposite: NZ:199 heads the 1-3-1 'widely described as the modern standard', and NZ:195 says the pure PASSIVE trap that is no longer viable is the 1-2-2 trap. zone_entries:748 meanwhile says a trap is 'most commonly a 1-3-1'. A viewer comes away with the reverse of the owner's picture. The 'most teams' claim is unsourced on both pages.

old: Options: Deep trap — all five back off and meet them at the blue line
new: Options: Deep trap — all five back off into your neutral-zone shape and meet them at your own blue line
note: Voiced alone, 'the blue line' could be either line, and 'trap' collides with NZ's trap, which kills at the RED line (NZ:164, :174). The body (:758) names both: 'meet the attack at the blue line… the forward on that side stands up and denies the red line'. The author must say which line, so the sketch's 'your own' is a guess. 122 chars of 200.

old: the other four flat across the ice at or near their own blue line
new: the other four flat across the ice at or near your own blue line
note: Throughout FS 'their' means the opponents ('their end', 'their net', 'their defence'). Voiced alone, 'their own blue line' can be heard as the opponents' line, the opposite end. FS:301 and the NZ owner (:268, nz-1-4 caption) both say 'your own blue line'. 0 chars net.

old: Never: Put two forwards in the same lane — one defender then covers both and you have made it 5-on-4 against yourself
new: Risk: Two forwards in one lane lets one defender cover both — unless your team stacks the middle on purpose in a 1-3-1 regroup, so ask
note: This states the spread as law. The stacked alternative is set out in puck_support_and_spacing.md:470/:476, glossary :98/:264, and the neutral-zone-lanes caption that NZ itself embeds at :640 ('the realistic alternative is a 1-3-1 regroup that deliberately stacks the middle lane… find out whether your team spreads or stacks'). So the page contradicts the diagram under it. NZ, which claims the regroups, never mentions a 1-3-1 regroup. The label change is a sketch; it may need to stay Never with a scope. ~135 of 200.

old: **One forward in each lane — left wall, middle, right wall — and hold your lane when the puck is in another.** Two in one lane lets one defender cover both.
new: **One forward in each lane — left wall, middle, right wall — and hold your lane when the puck is in another**, unless your team stacks the middle on a 1-3-1 regroup — ask. Two in one lane lets one defender cover both.
note: The same conflict as :630, in Key focus. Per CLAUDE.md, stating the tactic as the default is right; it needs the named alternative and an 'ask'. Low cost.

old: Against a 1-3-1, skate it out and go short up the wall, never through the middle.
new: Against a neutral-zone 1-3-1, skate it out and go short up the wall, never through the middle.
note: The 'Against each forecheck' section treats the 1-3-1 only as the passive neutral-zone wall ('one token forechecker', 'lots of time'). FS's pushed-up 1-3-1 forecheck brings its line of three, a defenceman included, into your end, where 'lots of time' does not hold.

old: If your team runs two defencemen (umbrella, 2-3)
new: If your team runs two defencemen (a classic umbrella, 2-3)

old: at or near **their own** blue line

note: The body twin of :462. The bold makes the ambiguous pronoun the stressed word.

The twin is :188, which partly self-corrects. Low consequence, because the instruction 'ask which end' survives.

old: **Umbrella** — a power-play structure with **three players high** across the top and two low, shaped like an umbrella canopy.

old: Alphabetical.
